brief.notification_title: Oil slides, stocks bounce 2%; crypto left behind
brief.market_summary: At midday, stocks are up sharply: S&P 500 +2.1% at 7,532, Nasdaq +2.5%, Russell 2000 +2.6%, SMH +4.5%. The trigger is Brent, down 4.5% to $93.93 after Qatar took an interim Iran proposal to reopen Hormuz to the White House. Nvidia is down 5–6% because its board is investigating Jensen Huang. Treasuries aren't joining in. The 5Y is up 2.3bp to 4.67% and the 10Y up 1.3bp to 4.87%, with December hike odds still high and the $125B refunding starting with today's 3-year auction. Crypto is the outlier: BTC is at $74,948 after a two-month low of $73,708, ETH is down 4.2% at $2,132, and about $1B of positions have been liquidated. AVAX (+7.2% on the NYSE news) is the exception. The week's real tests are still ahead: CPI and the 10-year auction on Tuesday, then Applied Materials and Cisco on Thursday.
brief.since_last: Sunday's brief was written over a quiet weekend. Since then: (1) Nvidia's board opened an investigation into Huang, which knocked Sunday-night futures down (Nasdaq 100 −0.8%). The cash session then turned the other way, and NVDA (−5–6%) is now dragging on a broad rally (n4, n71). (2) Qatar is taking an Iranian interim deal to the White House. Terms: Hormuz reopens, tanker attacks stop, the US blockade lifts and $8B of frozen funds is released. Neither government has confirmed, and Rubio says the sides are "not close." Brent fell through its 200-day average to $93.93 (n25, n74). (3) Crypto set new two-month lows on roughly $1B of long liquidations, and spot ETFs lost about $1.65B last week. NYSE picked Avalanche to settle tokenized stocks, and AVAX is +7.2% (n34, n105). (4) Before the open, Constellation (EPS $5.06 vs $3.85), NRG ($4.68 vs $3.33) and Ferguson (beat and raised, +12.5%) all beat. (5) Our XLK trim orders at $166.50 and $169 sit below today's $170.06 price, so they should have filled. The IEF and XLV bids have not.

economic_data.takeaway: China's factory-gate inflation is the highest in more than four years, while its consumer CPI is slowing (n175). Rising input costs abroad are another hawkish input for a Fed already priced for a December hike, and they work against the disinflation that cheaper oil brings.
I couldn't find the actual. Another print near 4% would support the hike case. Check it before the CPI, because the front end (5Y +2.3bp, 13-week bill +3.2bp) is already leaning hawkish today.

economic_data.when: Tue 10 Nov 08:30 ET (one calendar says Wed; confirm with BLS)
economic_data.takeaway: This is the last CPI before the 8–9 Dec FOMC. A print at or below 0.3% would ease the oil-driven September spike and could pull the 10Y toward 4.75%. A repeat of 0.5% or more would lock in a hike and push yields toward our IEF bid levels. Note: n128 ('Hot CPI seals rate hike') appears to describe the prior report, not October's.

This is the number that matters most. A 0.2% core reading would let the Fed frame December as one hike, which is bullish for duration and gives tech a chance to rebuild. A 0.4% reading would raise talk of a series of hikes, which is bearish for IEF, semis and crypto.
Claims are still very low, consistent with the +165k payroll beat. Only a jump above about 220K would change the labor story.
September's 1.3% was the oil shock. With Brent down about 10% in a week, November's pipeline pressure should ease, but October's print still reflects high energy prices.
A second 0.7% would show energy costs feeding into goods and services, the pass-through risk the Fed study flags (n20).

sections.summary: Lower oil has set off a broad relief rally. Every sector is up, led by semis (SMH +4.5%), industrials (+3.6%) and tech (+3.2%), and the VIX has dropped 18% to 20.9. Nvidia is the exception at −5–6% on the board's investigation of Huang, which a Democratic Congress is now positioned to turn into oversight. After last week's worst S&P week since April 2025, the index is still down 3.6% over the month and below its Election Day close.
key_points: SMH +4.5% today but −4.6% on the week and −19.7% on the month. AMD, AVGO and AMZN are each about +5% (Oppenheimer upgraded AMD). NVDA −5–6% (n71, n10).
Earnings: CEG, NRG and FERG all beat clearly. But S&P 500 companies are beating estimates by the narrowest margin in about four years (n122).
The VIX is 20.9, down from about 25.6, but still up 41% on the month. Volatility is still high, and sharp up days are common in this kind of market.

sections.summary: Treasuries are slightly weaker even with oil down 4.5%. Front-end yields are up most (13-week bill +3.2bp, 5Y +2.3bp, 30Y flat), reflecting December hike odds of about 65–78% and the start of the $125B refunding. The 10Y is still 37bp lower over the month after the Democratic sweep. Credit is firm: HYG +0.27%, LQD +0.08%.
key_points: Auctions: 3-year today at 1pm ET (prior auction 4.932%), $42B 10-year Tuesday on CPI day (October cleared at 5.300%, below the 5.317% when-issued yield), $25B 30-year Thursday.
Goldman sees the 10Y settling in a 4.75–5% range (n66). A Fed study says oil-shock pass-through to core inflation has doubled (n20).
IEF is at $91.72, above our $91.20 and $90.60 bids. Those would need the 10Y at roughly 4.95% and 5.05%.

sections.summary: Brent fell another 4.5% to $93.93, a two-month low below its 200-day average. That follows last week's 16–17% drop, the steepest since Covid, as Qatar takes an interim Iran proposal to the White House. The deal is not confirmed by either government, Rubio says the sides are 'not close', and over the weekend ships in Hormuz came under fire and the Houthis claimed a strike on Aramco's Riyadh offices. The trend is down, but the risk is headline-driven in both directions.
key_points: Murban rose 3.4% to $99.17 in Asia. The widening gap with Brent says the physical Gulf market is still tight.

Bank forecasts disagree: Goldman cut its forecasts on the Hormuz deal (n120); Citi raised its forecast and sees $150 if disruption persists (n118); Morgan Stanley raised (n152); Barclays holds $100 (n117).
Seven OPEC+ producers are keeping December output unchanged (n16). XLE is −7.5% on the week. OXY reports tonight.

sections.summary: Crypto missed the risk-on day completely. BTC hit a two-month low of $73,708 and is heading for a fifth straight weekly loss. ETH is down 4.2% after about $462M of long liquidations. ETF outflows (BTC −$1.18B and ETH −$365M last week) and the regulatory worries after the Democratic sweep matter more than the equity bounce. The NYSE's choice of Avalanche for tokenized-stock settlement is the one positive story, and AVAX is +7.2%.
key_points: About $1B of long liquidations across crypto (n105, n100). For ETH alone, $462M in 24 hours, 92% of it longs.
Strategy bought 1,036 BTC for $82M and now holds 850,364 (n85). But most of its $284M share sale is going to STRC buybacks rather than bitcoin (n2).
Binance's $6.3B hack: analysts see no contagion because Binance is covering user losses (n104). Schwab is adding SOL and AVAX (n61).

brief.instructor_take: The 2% bounce isn't what matters today. The week's real tests haven't happened yet: CPI and the 10-year auction on Tuesday, then AMAT and Cisco on Thursday. Most traders are reading cheaper oil as a clean win for stocks, but look at bonds. The 5-year is up 2.3bp and bills are up 3bp on a day Brent fell 4.5%. Rate traders still see a December hike and $125B of new supply, so I think equities are running ahead of what rates support. Second, when bitcoin and ether can't rally on a day the Nasdaq is up 2.5%, the problem is crypto's own flows, and I respect that signal. On oil, I'm not trading in either direction. The deal is unconfirmed, Rubio says 'not close', and Murban at $99 against Brent at $94 says the physical Gulf market hasn't relaxed. The next move depends on a headline I can't forecast. On positioning: our XLK trim should have filled into this strength, so the proceeds are in SGOV earning about 4% while we wait. Let the IEF and XLV bids work and don't chase. If core CPI prints 0.2% and the 10-year auction goes well, I'll look at rebuilding tech after AMAT. If CPI is hot, our bond bids fill at better yields. Either way the plan pays us for patience.

top_ideas.title: Buy 7–10Y Treasuries on a CPI/auction back-up
top_ideas.one_liner: Keep IEF bids at $91.20/$90.60 through CPI and 10Y auction
top_ideas.thesis: This week brings $125B of supply and the last CPI before the December FOMC. That's a good setup for the 10Y to rise briefly toward 4.95–5.05%, the top of the 4.75–5% range Goldman expects. Over months, falling oil and a Democratic Congress lean toward lower long yields, so I want to buy duration on weakness, not at today's 4.87%.
top_ideas.reasoning: The evidence is split, and that argues for patient limit bids rather than buying at market. On the hawkish side, payrolls were +165k against about 60k expected, December hike odds are about 65–78% (n158), and a Fed study says oil shocks now feed into core inflation twice as fast (n20). That's why the 5-year is up today even with Brent down 4.5%. On the other side, the 10Y has already fallen 37bp in a month after the Democratic sweep, Brent just broke its 200-day average, and Goldman sees 10s settling at 4.75–5% (n66). I choose the 7–10 year part of the curve because it captures most of the gain if growth slows or the Fed hikes once and stops, without the 30-year's exposure to fiscal and term-premium risk. My bids at $91.20 and $90.60 correspond to roughly 4.95% and 5.05% on the 10Y. This week gives the market three chances to get there: today's 3-year auction, CPI and the $42B 10-year on Tuesday, and the 30-year on Thursday. Less experienced investors often miss that yields tend to rise ahead of big auctions whatever the macro news. That temporary price discount is what I'm trying to buy. I'm wrong if the 10Y closes above 5.20%, or if CPI and the Fed speakers present December as the first of several hikes. If the 10Y falls below 4.75% before the bids fill, I cancel instead of chasing.

top_ideas.title: Don't chase the semis bounce before AMAT
top_ideas.one_liner: Don't chase the chip bounce; wait for AMAT Thursday
top_ideas.thesis: SMH's +4.5% day is a relief rally driven by cheaper oil and short-covering after a −13% week. It's not a change in the rate or earnings backdrop. Keep the XLK trim proceeds in SGOV until CPI and Applied Materials' guidance on Thursday show whether the bounce has substance.
top_ideas.reasoning: I read today as a relief rally, not a turn. The catalyst was oil, and SOXX had fallen 13% the week before, so shorts had plenty to cover. Even after today SMH is −4.6% on the week and −19.7% on the month. Three things haven't changed. The Fed is still priced to hike in December, S&P earnings beats are the narrowest in about four years (n122), and Nvidia, the largest weight in SMH, now has a governance problem that a Democratic Congress wants to investigate (n10, n71). The VIX is down 18% today but still up 41% on the month, and high-volatility markets are exactly where rallies like this happen. We trimmed XLK into this move at $166.50–169. Buying semis back a day before CPI and three days before AMAT would undo that discipline at a worse price. AMAT on Thursday (estimate $4.06 vs $2.17 a year ago) is the right test, because it shows whether chip-equipment spending holds up as data-center construction slows (n3). I'd change my mind if SMH closes back above about $508, its level a week ago, after AMAT guides higher and core CPI comes in at 0.2% or lower. In that case I'd buy back the trimmed slice in two halves.

top_ideas.title: Trim ether into bounces as ETF outflows persist
top_ideas.one_liner: Sell a third of ETH into any bounce to $2,250–2,300
top_ideas.thesis: ETH fell 4.2% on a strong risk-on day for stocks, after $365M of spot ETF outflows last week and $462M of long liquidations. When an asset can't rally with everything else, the problem is its own flows. ETH is the weakest of the large layer-1 tokens, so that's where to cut risk, using limit sells into a bounce rather than selling at the lows.
top_ideas.reasoning: Crypto is telling us something equities aren't. On a day the Nasdaq is up 2.5%, BTC is down 1% and ETH down 4.2%. When an asset can't rally on a broad risk-on day, the cause is usually its own flows, and the flows here are poor. Spot ETH ETFs lost $365M last week, with BlackRock's ETHA alone losing $91M on Friday. About $462M of ETH longs were liquidated in 24 hours, and the Glamsterdam testnet fork was delayed. BTC at least has a regular buyer in Strategy (1,036 BTC, n85). But Strategy sent most of its new $284M raise to STRC buybacks rather than bitcoin (n2), which suggests the corporate bid is thinning. ETH is the weaker of the two (−14% on the month vs −9% for BTC), so that's where I'd reduce. I don't want to sell at a liquidation low. Short squeezes like BTC's 1.2% jump in one hour (n19) are common in this market, so I'd place limit sells into a bounce. I'm wrong if ETH closes above $2,400 and ETH ETF flows turn positive for several sessions. A hot CPI is a downside risk, and a soft one could deliver the bounce I'm selling into.
catalysts: Daily spot ETH and BTC ETF flow data (no Monday data yet)
Crypto regulatory signals from the new Democratic Congress
risks: A soft CPI sets off a sharp short squeeze, and ETH runs past $2,400 before or after we sell

top_ideas.entry: Place GTC limit sells for one-third of your ETH (spot or ETHA): half at $2,250 and half at $2,300, good through Fri 20 Nov. Backstop: if ETH has a daily close below $2,000 before they fill, sell the unfilled part the next day. Proceeds go to SGOV.
top_ideas.invalidation: ETH closes above $2,400 and spot ETH ETFs show three straight sessions of inflows. Cancel the unfilled sells.
top_ideas.sizing: Trim one-third of ETH holdings; keep total crypto at 3–5% of the portfolio or less

lesson.explanation: When the Treasury is about to sell a lot of new debt, dealers and investors often let yields rise (prices fall) in the days before the auction. That makes room on their balance sheets and gets them a better price on the new bonds. If demand at the auction is strong, yields often ease afterward. A 'stop-through' means the auction cleared below the when-issued yield (strong demand); a 'tail' means it cleared above it (weak demand). For a buyer, the days before an auction are often the cheapest time to buy duration.
lesson.todays_example: This week's $125B refunding starts with the 3-year today, then the $42B 10-year on Tuesday, the same day as CPI, and the $25B 30-year on Thursday. Yields are up 1–2bp today even though Brent fell 4.5%, which looks like supply pressure. Our IEF bids sit about 8–17bp above the current 10Y yield to catch that discount. October's 10-year cleared at 5.300%, below the 5.317% when-issued yield.
